transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I came in because I’ve been having this problem when people ask me something simple, and I can’t seem to just answer the simple thing. Like at work, someone will ask me when a ring repair will be ready, and instead of saying, you know, “Thursday” or “I’ll check,” my answer starts wandering all over the place. I’ll start with the invoice, then somehow I’m talking about garden soil, and then mortgage papers, and while I’m talking I can see their face kind of… go blank. Like they’re losing me, or I’m losing them.

It’s embarrassing, because in my head it feels connected while it’s happening, but then I hear myself and I think, why did I say all that? They only asked about a ring. It’s been making it hard to deal with customers, and I thought I should come in before it gets worse or before I make a bigger mess of things.
Do you feel anxious or stressed when you're talking to customers and your answers start wandering off topic?

Yes, I do get stressed, but it’s sort of because I can feel it happening while I’m talking. Like they’ll ask something very ordinary, “When will this ring be ready?” and I know the answer should be short, but then I start explaining the invoice, and then my mind jumps to something like garden soil, and then somehow I’m mentioning mortgage papers, and I can see their expression change.

That’s the part that makes me anxious—the moment I notice I’ve lost them. I’ll think, why am I talking about this? They just wanted a date. And then I get more flustered, and it’s harder to pull myself back to the actual question.
Does this happen to you in all conversations, or is it mostly when you're talking to customers at work?

Mostly with customers at work, I think… or at least that’s where I notice it the most, because there’s pressure to give a clear answer. Like they’ll ask something simple, “When will my ring repair be ready?” and I know I should just say the date or say I’ll check the invoice, but then I’ll start talking about the invoice, and somehow I’m off into garden soil or mortgage papers, and by then I can see their face change, like they’re not following me anymore.

It probably happens in other conversations too, maybe a little, but at work it stands out because the question is so straightforward and I still can’t keep my answer in a straight line.
Are you noticing any difficulties in your personal relationships or daily activities outside of work due to this issue with your conversations?

Yes… yes, it’s definitely starting to affect things outside of just talking to customers, though work is still where it shows the most. I’ve had to cut back on custom pieces, which is hard for me to admit, because that used to be the part I felt most confident about. Sitting with someone and figuring out exactly what they wanted, the stone, the setting, the little details—that was something I could do. But lately during consultations I lose track of what they’re asking for, or I’ll start explaining one part and drift into another, and then I’m not sure I captured the actual request correctly.

And then with repairs, I’ve missed deadlines. Not constantly, but enough that it scares me. I’ll think I’ve written everything down or that I know where we are in the process, and then I realize the date passed or I misunderstood what step needed to happen next. So now I take fewer of those jobs because I don’t want to disappoint people or ruin someone’s trust.

At home, my husband has been double-checking invoices for me. That’s embarrassing because I used to handle all of that myself without thinking twice. Now I’ll ask him to look over them because I’m worried I put the wrong thing down or left something out after a conversation went sideways. It makes me feel like I’m losing pieces of what I used to be able to manage.
Do you find yourself having trouble focusing on a single task for an extended period of time?

Yes… I mean, I think that’s part of it, but it shows up most clearly when I’m trying to answer someone. It’s not always like I sit down at the bench and immediately can’t do one thing—though sometimes I do feel scattered—but the reason I came in is more that when someone asks me something simple, like, “When will this ring repair be ready?” I should just be able to say the date or say I’ll check.

Instead my answer starts stretching out. I’ll mention the invoice, then I’m explaining something about the order, and then somehow my mind has jumped to garden soil or mortgage papers, things that have nothing to do with the customer’s question. And I can hear myself doing it, almost like I’m watching it happen, but I can’t always stop it fast enough. Then I see the person’s face change, like they’re trying to follow me but they can’t, and I realize I’ve lost the thread.

So yes, focusing on one thing is hard, but it’s especially hard keeping my thoughts in one straight line when I’m speaking.
Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you have trouble keeping your thoughts on track in conversations with friends or family?

Yes… I do get overwhelmed, especially because I can tell it’s happening while it’s happening. It’s not just that I forget a word or get a little distracted. It’s more like someone asks me something simple, and I know there should be a simple answer, but my mind doesn’t stay on that one track.

Like with the ring repairs—someone asks when it’ll be ready, and I start with the repair date or the invoice, and then somehow I’m talking about the invoice details, and then my head jumps to garden soil or mortgage papers or something that has nothing to do with what they asked. And I can see the other person’s face change, like they’re trying to be polite but they’re losing me, and then I feel embarrassed and tense because I know I’m not making sense the way I meant to.

With friends or family it’s a little less formal than with customers, but yes, I still feel that pressure once I notice I’ve gone off somewhere else. I start trying to pull myself back, and sometimes that makes me even more flustered.
Did you have difficulties with focusing or following conversations when you were a child?

Not that I remember as a child, no… at least not in this same way. I mean, I wasn’t perfect, I’m sure I daydreamed like any kid, but I don’t remember people looking at me like they couldn’t follow what I was saying.

This feels different to me because now it happens right in the middle of ordinary conversations. Like I came in because someone asks me something simple—when a ring repair will be ready, something I should be able to answer clearly—and then my answer starts wandering. I’ll begin with the date or the invoice, then I’m talking about invoice details, and somehow my mind jumps to garden soil, or mortgage papers, or something completely unrelated. And I can see them losing me while I’m still talking.

So… no, I don’t think this was a childhood thing, or at least I don’t remember it that way. This is something I’m noticing now because it’s interfering with conversations I used to handle without trouble.
Did you experience any significant difficulties with learning or paying attention in school?

I don’t really remember having major trouble in school that way. I mean, school wasn’t always easy, and I wasn’t some perfect student who loved every subject, but I don’t have a memory of teachers saying I couldn’t pay attention or that I couldn’t follow what was being taught.

I did some college later, so I must have been able to manage it well enough. If anything, I remember certain classes being harder depending on whether I was interested or whether the teacher explained things in a way that made sense to me, but I think that’s probably true for a lot of people. I’m not sure I’d call it a significant learning problem.

So… no, not that I can point to. I don’t think there was some big school pattern like that, at least not one I’m aware of.
Did you experience any difficulties with speech or language development as a child?

I don’t think so… not that anyone ever told me, anyway. I don’t remember having speech therapy or being pulled aside for language problems, or anything like that.

Of course, I only know so much from being a child, and my memory of those early years isn’t perfect. But from what I’ve been told, I talked normally enough, learned to read and write normally enough, and I don’t remember teachers or family making a big issue of how I spoke.

So… no, I don’t have anything specific there. Nothing I can point to as a childhood speech or language difficulty.
Did your symptoms start after something significant happened in your life?

Yes… I think it did, or at least that’s when I really started noticing that something had shifted.

It was not long after we took on the business mortgage. I keep coming back to that because before then, I felt like I was managing things in the usual way, and then after that, gradually, everything felt different. Not all at once like a switch flipping, but close enough in time that I connect the two in my mind.

That mortgage was a big thing for us—the kind of decision where it’s not just paperwork, it feels like the whole business and future are sitting on top of it. And this whole change has been going on since around then… almost two years now. I don’t know if that caused it exactly, but the timing lines up.
Did you notice your symptoms worsening or improving when the stress related to the business mortgage changed, such as during periods of financial stability or instability?

I’m not really sure I can map it that cleanly, honestly. I mean, I’ve thought about that because it would make sense, right—if the money side felt calmer, maybe I’d feel calmer, and if things felt shaky, maybe I’d get worse. But when I try to look back at it, it’s kind of muddled.

There were times when the business felt a little more stable, or at least not actively on fire, and I don’t know that I can say, “Oh yes, that’s when everything improved.” And there were stressful periods too, but I’m not sure I noticed a clear worsening that lined up exactly with those. It’s more like the mortgage became this background pressure that was just… there. Even when things weren’t immediately bad, I still felt aware of it, like it was sitting in the room with us.

So I guess my answer is: I haven’t noticed a definite pattern. I connect the beginning of things with that whole period, but I can’t say the symptoms reliably went up or down depending on whether the finances were better or worse. It wasn’t that obvious to me.
Did you experience any difficulties with organization or time management as a child?

I’m not really sure. Nothing stands out to me from childhood in that way, at least not as something people pointed to as a problem.

I mean, I wasn’t perfect—I don’t think any child is. I’m sure I misplaced things sometimes or procrastinated on homework here and there, but I don’t remember teachers saying I had a real issue with organization or being on time. I don’t remember my parents being especially worried about that, either.

It’s hard because looking back that far, you sort of have to piece it together from little memories and what other people told you. But no, I don’t have a clear memory of struggling with time management or organization as a child in any serious or unusual way.
Do you think your symptoms of wandering off topic in conversations are always triggered by feelings of stress or anxiety?

No, I don’t think it’s always stress or anxiety. I mean, stress probably makes it worse sometimes, because if I’m already tense I feel like my thoughts sort of scatter more easily. But it happens even during ordinary conversations, too.

That’s actually part of why I came in. Someone will ask me something simple at the shop, like when a ring repair will be ready, and I’ll start answering, but then somehow I’m talking about the invoices, and then that reminds me of the soil I need for the garden, and then suddenly I’m thinking about the mortgage papers. And I can see the person’s face change, like they’re trying to follow me but I’ve lost the thread. Then I realize I haven’t actually answered the question they asked.

So… no, I wouldn’t say it’s only triggered by stress. It can happen with a very normal question, which is embarrassing, honestly, because I know the answer should be straightforward.
Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or experience symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity as a child or adolescent?

No, not that I know of. I was never diagnosed with ADHD as a child or teenager, at least nobody ever told me that or had me evaluated for it.

As far as symptoms back then… I don’t really remember anything that would clearly fit that. I mean, I had normal kid moments, I’m sure—getting distracted, not wanting to do homework, maybe talking when I shouldn’t—but I don’t remember it being treated like a serious problem. I wasn’t the kid who was always being sent out of class or constantly in trouble for not sitting still, at least not in my memory.

And my parents didn’t talk about me that way either, like, “Oh, you could never focus” or “you were impossible to manage.” So I guess I’d say no known diagnosis, and I don’t have a clear memory of inattention or hyperactivity or impulsivity being a major issue when I was younger.
Are there areas in your daily life outside of work where you feel like your conversations are causing problems or making it hard for you to connect with others?

Yes, I think so. Work is where I notice it the most because customers need clear answers, but it doesn’t only happen there.

Even outside work, if someone asks me something simple, I can start out trying to answer and then I sort of drift sideways. Like I’ll be asked one thing, and then I’m suddenly talking about something only partly related, and then another thing after that. It reminds me of what I was saying about the ring repairs—someone asks when something will be ready, and somehow I’m on invoices, then garden soil, then mortgage papers, and I can see in their face that I’ve lost them.

That’s the part that bothers me, really. It’s not that I’m trying to ignore people or be difficult. I feel like I am answering, but then I realize I’ve gone around the block and never actually said the thing they asked. And then I get embarrassed and try to pull it back, but by then the conversation feels awkward. So yes, it does make connecting with people harder sometimes, because I can tell they’re waiting for me to land the plane, so to speak.
Do you find that your conversations wander off topic in the same way when you're speaking with close friends or family members, compared to when you're speaking with customers at work?

Yes, it can happen with friends or family too, though I notice it more at work because customers are looking for a direct answer and I can see right away when I’m not giving one.

With family, they might be more patient, or they’ll interrupt me and say, “Wait, what are you talking about?” But it’s the same kind of thing. Someone asks me something simple, and I start off in the right place, and then my mind sort of takes side roads. Like with the ring repair example I mentioned — someone asks when it’ll be ready, and I’m trying to answer that, but then I’m thinking about the invoice, and then that somehow reminds me of needing garden soil, and then I’m thinking about mortgage papers. And by then I can tell I’ve completely lost the person.

It’s embarrassing because I don’t mean to do it. I’m not trying to avoid the question. I feel like I’m explaining, but then I realize I’ve gone too far away from what they actually asked. So yes, close people see it too, just maybe they’re more used to me and less formal about pointing it out.
Did your difficulties with staying on topic in conversations or following through on tasks start before the age of 16?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I don’t have a clear memory of it being a problem before I was 16, at least not in the way I notice it now.

I mean, I can remember being a teenager and having normal distractions or not always finishing things right away, but I don’t remember people making a big issue out of me not staying on topic or not being able to follow through. Nobody sat me down and said, you know, “You’re always wandering off in conversations,” or “You can’t complete anything.” If it was happening, I don’t think it was obvious enough that it stood out to me.

So I guess my best answer is: I can’t really say it started before 16. I don’t have that memory or evidence of it from back then. It’s more something I’m aware of as an adult, especially when other people seem confused by what I’m saying.
Did your difficulties with conversations and staying on topic start suddenly or have they been gradually worsening over time?

I don’t think it was sudden, like one day I woke up and couldn’t answer people clearly. It feels more like it’s been creeping up, or maybe I’ve just become more aware of it because people react to it.

The reason I came in, really, is because it started becoming obvious in conversations. Someone will ask me a simple question, like when a ring repair is going to be ready, and I’ll begin trying to answer that, but then my mind catches on the invoice, and from there I’m talking about something else entirely, like garden soil I meant to buy, and then somehow mortgage papers. And while I’m saying it, part of me thinks it all connects, but then I can see the other person’s face change, like they’re waiting for me to get back to the actual answer.

So I’d say it’s been gradually more noticeable over time, not sudden. It’s just gotten to the point where I can’t brush it off as much, because I can see people losing me.
Did your parents or teachers ever mention that you had difficulty with self-regulation of emotions or behaviors as a child?

I don’t really know that they did, no. I’m trying to think back carefully, because childhood memories can get kind of blurry, and I don’t want to just give you an answer because it sounds neat.

I don’t remember teachers calling my parents in about me being unable to control my emotions or my behavior. I mean, I’m sure I had moments like any kid—getting upset, being stubborn, talking when I shouldn’t, that sort of thing—but nothing stands out as a pattern that adults were pointing out. My parents didn’t have some repeated phrase like, “You’re out of control,” or “You can’t manage yourself,” at least not that I remember.

If anything, I remember the usual corrections kids get, but I don’t have a clear memory of anyone identifying it as a real difficulty. So my honest answer is I’m not sure, but I don’t recall parents or teachers specifically mentioning problems with self-regulation when I was a child.
Did any of your relatives, such as parents or siblings, have difficulties with attention or behavior that were similar to what you're experiencing now?

I’m not really sure. I can’t think of anyone in my immediate family who had the same kind of thing, at least not in a way that was talked about clearly.

My parents had their own habits and ways of doing things, and my siblings too, but I don’t remember anyone being described as having attention problems or behavior problems like what you’re asking. Not that I know of. I mean, families don’t always label things that way, especially when I was younger, so it’s possible I missed something or it just wasn’t discussed.

But if you’re asking whether I know of a parent or sibling who had similar trouble staying on track or following through in the way I’m dealing with now, I’d have to say no, not that I’m aware of.
